guide.summary: Slack uses a standard v2 OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, and creating an app and getting a token in your own workspace is quick. Reaching other workspaces is the hard part. An app that has not been distributed only installs in the workspace where it was created. Slack's terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercial distribution. Unlisted distributed apps are meant for testing, and new non-Marketplace commercial installs are limited to 1 request per minute on conversations.history and conversations.replies. That limit hurts any agent that reads message history. Marketplace inclusion is free but requires a security and scope review, and no claim states how long that review takes. Slack's Developer Policy also bans using Slack data to train an LLM under any circumstances.

reasons_to_bring_own: Slack's API Terms treat the Marketplace as the only appropriate channel for commercially distributing Slack apps, so shipping a commercial product under your own name eventually means your own app going through Marketplace review.

New installs of commercially distributed non-Marketplace apps are capped at 1 request per minute and 15 objects per request on conversations.history and conversations.replies. A Marketplace-listed app of your own is the documented way out of that cap.
An internal app built inside your own workspace keeps the higher limits of 50+ requests per minute and up to 1,000 objects per request, which suits single-workspace internal use.
GovSlack customers authorize on a separate host (slack-gov.com), and the Composio info does not say whether managed auth covers it.
build_or_borrow.verdict: Use Composio managed auth to start; you do not need your own app yet because, outside your own workspace, Slack's path for your own app runs through distribution and Marketplace review with no documented timeline, plus tight rate limits on history reads until you are listed.

prerequisites.text: A Slack account and a workspace where you can create the app at the App Management page (api.slack.com/apps). Until it is distributed, the app only installs in that workspace.
An HTTPS redirect URL, configured under OAuth & Permissions.
For Marketplace listing, Slack publishes a page of prerequisites the app must meet before review, but its contents were not captured. Read it before planning a launch date.

oauth.token_lifetime: Tokens do not expire by default. If you turn on optional token rotation, you get an expiring access token plus a refresh token. The temporary authorization code expires after ten minutes.
redirect_uri_rules: Configure Redirect URLs under OAuth & Permissions in the app settings.
The redirect_uri must match a configured Redirect URL or be a subdirectory of one, so matching is not strictly exact.
Redirect URLs cannot contain an anchor (#).

blockers.text: An undistributed app only installs in the workspace where it was created, so your users' workspaces cannot connect until you distribute it.
blockers.workaround: Use Composio managed auth for other workspaces. Use your own undistributed app only for testing in your own workspace.

blockers.text: Commercial distribution is expected to go through the Marketplace, and the Marketplace requires a security review plus a check of your scopes against your app's functionality. No claim documents how long the review takes.
blockers.workaround: Ship on Composio managed auth now and start the Marketplace submission early, requesting only the scopes your features need.

blockers.text: New installs of commercially distributed non-Marketplace apps (from May 29, 2025) get 1 request per minute and 15 objects per request on conversations.history and conversations.replies.
blockers.workaround: Get listed on the Marketplace, or use an internal app inside a single workspace, which keeps 50+ requests per minute and up to 1,000 objects per request. Existing installs of unlisted distributed apps are not affected.

blockers.text: A published app fails to install with unapproved_scope if it requests scopes that are still in review or were never submitted.
blockers.workaround: Submit every scope you plan to request for review before adding it to the published install flow.

app_specific_gotchas.text: The Developer Policy prohibits using Slack data to train an LLM under any circumstances. Keep Slack content out of any training or fine-tuning pipeline.
Reading message history is throttled to 1 request per minute with at most 15 objects for new commercial installs of non-Marketplace apps. An agent that summarizes channels will crawl.
Scopes are additive. You cannot reduce a token's scopes without revoking it, so over-asking early sticks.
Bot scopes go in the scope parameter and user scopes go in a separate user_scope parameter.
GovSlack workspaces authorize on slack-gov.com instead of slack.com.

paths.verdict: Easy, same day. The developer creates the app and installs it in the workspace where it was created, with no review. The catch is that it only works in that one workspace. Treat this path as a prototype or as a single-customer build, not as the product. Internal apps keep the higher history limits.

unapproved_mode.breaks_at: There are two break points. First, installing into any workspace other than the creating one fails while the app is undistributed. Second, once the app is published, any install requesting a scope still in review or never submitted fails with unapproved_scope.

steps.title: Decide how the app will be distributed
steps.detail_md:
This choice decides who can install the app and what limits apply, so **you** make it. The agent can only lay out the trade-offs:

- **Internal, undistributed app:** installs only in the workspace where it was created (c9). Internal customer-built apps keep the higher limits: 50+ requests per minute and up to 1,000 objects per request (c31).
- **Unlisted distributed app:** meant for development and testing, not large-scale or commercial distribution (c28). Slack's updated API Terms say the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercial distribution, including unlisted apps (c27).
  - New commercially distributed non-Marketplace apps, and new installs of existing ones, are capped at 1 request per minute and 15 objects per request on conversations.history and conversations.replies. This applies from May 29, 2025 (c25, c29).
  - Existing installs of unlisted distributed apps are not subject to the new limits (c30).
- **Marketplace:** the Developer Policy says apps intended for commercial distribution at scale should be submitted for review (c34).
  - You cannot list on the Marketplace while also offering customers a parallel unlisted or custom app that violates Marketplace guidelines (c36).

For an AI agent that reads message history for many customers, the non-Marketplace history limit is crippling, so plan on the Marketplace.

Also note: the Developer Policy prohibits using Data to train an LLM under any circumstances (c35). Confirm your product complies before building.

Composio's static directory lists a Slack toolkit with managed auth. If you rely on it, the distribution rules above still apply to whichever app is used.

steps.title: Create the Slack app in App Management
steps.detail_md:
1. Log in at api.slack.com/apps (the page was reachable, c38) and create the app.
2. Note the client ID on the App Management page (c4). The client secret is needed later for the code exchange (c5).
3. Decide whether you target GovSlack. GovSlack apps use a separate authorize host, slack-gov.com instead of slack.com (c3, c14).

steps.title: Draft the minimal scope list
steps.detail_md:
The agent drafts the scope list, split into two groups:

- **Bot scopes** go in the `scope` parameter.
- **User scopes** go in the `user_scope` parameter (c19).

Keep the list minimal. Scopes are additive across installs and cannot be reduced on a token without revoking it (c8, c20).

Mark nice-to-have scopes as optional by unchecking them in app settings. Admins pre-approve optional scopes (c12).

For each scope, write a one-line justification tied to a feature. Marketplace review analyzes requested scopes against the app's functionality (c33).

The specific scope names your agent needs are not covered by the provided claims. Choose them from the features you actually ship.

steps.title: List redirect URLs
steps.detail_md:
The agent lists every callback URL for dev, staging and prod. Each one must meet these rules:

- Must use HTTPS (c7, c17).
- Must not contain an anchor (#) (c18).
- The `redirect_uri` sent at runtime must match a configured Redirect URL or be a subdirectory of it (c18).

Prefer exact, separate entries over broad parent paths.

steps.title: Enter redirect URLs and scopes in the app settings
steps.detail_md:
In the app's settings under **OAuth & Permissions** (c7):

1. Add the redirect URLs from step 4.
2. Add the scopes from step 3, unchecking any that should be optional (c12).
3. Copy the client ID and client secret into your secrets store (c4, c5).

steps.title: Implement the OAuth v2 flow
steps.detail_md:
The agent writes the integration code for Slack's v2 OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow (c1, c13).

1. **Authorize:** redirect users to https://slack.com/oauth/v2/authorize, or the slack-gov.com host for GovSlack (c2, c14). Pass bot scopes in `scope` and user scopes in `user_scope` (c19).
2. **Exchange:** send the code to oauth.v2.access at https://slack.com/api/oauth.v2.access using the client secret (c5, c15). The code expires after ten minutes, so exchange it immediately (c6, c16).
3. **Tokens:** by default tokens do not expire. Token rotation is optional and gives a refresh token plus an expiring access token (c21). If you enable rotation, build refresh handling.
4. **PKCE:** the OIDC discovery document does not advertise PKCE methods (c39). Do not depend on PKCE without confirming it.
5. **Rate limits:** limits apply per method, per workspace, per app. Tier 2 allows 20+ requests per minute (c23). Honor HTTP 429 and the Retry-After header (c24).
6. **Errors:** handle `unapproved_scope` explicitly (c22).

steps.title: Test-install in your own workspace
steps.detail_md:
Install the app in the workspace where it was created. This is the only place an undistributed app can be installed (c9).

Then check the full flow:

- The authorize page loads. A probe of the authorize endpoint returned HTTP 200 (c40).
- The code exchange succeeds within ten minutes (c6).
- Both bot and user tokens arrive with the expected scopes.

steps.title: Prepare Marketplace submission materials
steps.detail_md:
The agent drafts:

- The app description.
- A scope-by-scope justification mapped to features. Review analyzes scopes against functionality and includes a security review (c26, c33).

There is no fee for Marketplace inclusion (c26, c32).

The specific review prerequisites are listed on Slack's Marketplace review process page, but that content was not captured (c37). Read that page yourself before submitting.

steps.title: Submit the app for Marketplace review
steps.detail_md: Log in and submit the app for review. Confirm it meets the prerequisites on the Marketplace review process page (c37) and the Developer Policy, including the LLM-training prohibition (c35, c34).

steps.title: Wait for Slack's security and scope review
steps.detail_md:
Slack runs a security review and analyzes your scopes against the app's functionality (c33).

**How long this takes is not documented in the available claims (c37).** The estimate of 0 minutes below means unknown, not instant.

While scopes are in review, installs of the published app requesting them fail with `unapproved_scope` (c10, c22).

steps.title: Verify installs in other workspaces and orgs
steps.detail_md:
After approval, install the app in a second workspace and confirm there are no `unapproved_scope` errors (c22).

If you later add scopes, they need review again. Installs requesting unapproved scopes fail (c10).

For Enterprise customers, org-level installs may require an Org Owner or Admin when the app is already installed on individual workspaces (c11). Tell customers this up front.

belief_diff.topic: Does letting arbitrary users connect require provider review or verification?
belief_diff.prior_belief: Yes, for public distribution Slack requires the app to go through its App Directory review process before arbitrary workspaces can install it, while unlisted internal installs need no review.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say Marketplace listing requires a security review and scope analysis, and that the Marketplace is the only appropriate channel for commercial distribution, including unlisted apps; unlisted apps are meant only for development and testing. Claims do not say unlisted internal installs need no review, and they contradict the idea that unlisted apps can serve arbitrary workspaces.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Slack's App Directory review typically takes about 2 to 4 weeks from submission to a decision.
belief_diff.finding: The claims explicitly state that the wait times were not captured and do not give a review duration.

belief_diff.topic: Limits while the app is unapproved
belief_diff.prior_belief: While unapproved, an app can be installed only into the workspace of its developer or into workspaces that have explicitly been granted access, with a cap of 25 installs under the unlisted distribution model.
belief_diff.finding: Claims say undistributed apps can only be installed in the workspace where they were created, which contradicts the allowance for explicitly granted workspaces; no claim mentions a 25-install cap.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Slack charges no fee to create or distribute an app, and listing in the App Directory is free.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm Slack charges no fee for Marketplace inclusion, but say nothing about fees for creating or distributing an app outside the Marketplace.

belief_diff.topic: Key prerequisites (domain, privacy policy, video, business verification)
belief_diff.prior_belief: A public listing requires a verified publisher domain, a publicly accessible privacy policy URL, support contact details, and a demo video, while business verification is not required for listing.
belief_diff.finding: The claims state that the Marketplace review prerequisites were not fetched and are not captured, so domain, privacy policy, video, and business verification requirements are not addressed.

belief_diff.prior_belief: Slack requires every OAuth redirect URL to use HTTPS, be registered in the app settings beforehand, and match exactly with no wildcard or localhost exceptions except that http localhost is permitted for development.
belief_diff.finding: Claims confirm HTTPS and registration under OAuth & Permissions, but state that redirect_uri matching allows subdirectories of a configured URL, so it is not purely exact; claims do not mention a localhost exception.
